title: Phone Bans Are Healthy for All of Us Full Stop
author: Chelsea DeLorme
source: First Fish Substack (testimony before Maine joint committees), February 23, 2026
summary: Chelsea DeLorme's testimony before Maine's joint Appropriations & Financial Affairs / Education & Cultural Affairs committee in support of the Phone-Free Schools for ME bill. Her central reframing: The Anxious Generation describes parents — anxious for good reason, with bad results — and our kids are the Avoidance Generation, because avoidance is how anxiety shows up behaviorally. Avoidance is easy, convenient, and comfortable, but it's the opposite of learning, and a lifetime of it isn't life at all. Friction is inherent to learning across math class, the hallway, and the cafeteria, and kids need adult support to face it. DeLorme exposes the framing trap in school surveys ('Do you support a bell-to-bell ban during the school day?') versus the right question ('If none of your classmates had a phone during the school day, would you be OK without one too?'), arguing parents are caught in a collective-action trap and need schools to help break it. She names the simple substitution test: phones are social media, social media is phones — anytime someone argues for an exception, replace 'phone' with 'social media' and listen to how it sounds. Her closing reframe addresses the school-shooting fear directly: she doesn't want her kids texting in a crisis; she wants them alert, listening to and trusting their teacher, knowing the invisible string connecting them is more important and powerful than a smartphone.
points: Reframe the generation: The Anxious Generation describes the parents (anxious for good reason, with bad results); kids are the Avoidance Generation because avoidance is how anxiety shows up behaviorally — easy, convenient, comfortable, and the opposite of learning.

Survey framing matters: 'Do you support a bell-to-bell ban?' is the wrong question; 'If none of your classmates had a phone during the school day, would you be OK without one?' is the right one, and the answer is yes.
Parents are caught in a collective-action trap of their own creation; schools have to help break it because individual parental boundaries are unsustainable against the surrounding culture.
The substitution test: phones are social media, social media is phones — anytime someone argues for a phone exception, replace 'phone' with 'social media' and the case usually collapses.

On safety: a 6-7 hour break from phones at school is one of the most cost-effective rapid interventions, especially for students struggling to reach their potential, and the school-shooting-text fear cuts the wrong way (you want kids alert and trusting their teacher, not heads down on a screen).
quotes: My personal epiphany in reading 'Anxious Generation' was that the moniker doesn't refer to our kids, it refers to us, their parents. Anxious often for good reason, with bad results.

Our kids are the Avoidance Generation. Avoidance is how anxiety shows up through behavior. Avoidance is easy. Avoidance is convenient. Avoidance is comfortable. And avoidance is not a healthy habit for adults to accommodate. Because avoidance is the opposite of learning. And a lifetime of avoidance isn't life at all.

Friction is inherent to learning, whether that learning is in math class, the hallway, or in the cafeteria, academic, emotional or social. Our kids need support to face friction. Many of them want it.

Too often high schoolers have been asked: Do you support a bell-to-bell ban during the school day? when that is NOT the question. The real question is: If none of your classmates had a phone during the school day would you be OK without one too? (The answer is: They would be. They are.)

We are currently in a collective action trap of our own creation and parents need schools to help get us out. The research base has caught up with common sense and across the past year it has become common knowledge: Phone bans are healthy for all of us. Full stop.

To simplify the issue: Phones are social media. Social media is phones. Anytime someone argues for having a phone during the school day or creating an exception beyond a 504, IEP or medically prescribed use, replace the word phone with social media and see how that sounds.

School shootings scare me too. But no, I don't want my kids texting me in a time of crisis. I want them to be alert, I want them to listen to and trust their teacher. And I want them to already know how much they are loved every time they walk out of our porch door.” Archived from First Fish Substack (testimony before Maine joint committees) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
